answer.evidence: The image is a full opaque 96x96 ground tile: speckled dirt with an L-shaped asphalt road (a vertical arm at about x=55-82 from row 18, and a horizontal arm at about x=5-83 from row 50 to row 77). It is not the small 4px corner bite the name describes. Everything is a flat plan view seen from above, with no ellipse, no front-edge line with a front face below it, and no roof. The only vertical-looking part is a 1-3 row dark brown ledge under the south edge of the road (rows 76-78), which is a thin edge shadow and not a front face of 3+ rows. There is no side face. So it reads as a flat top-down slab, which is consistent with the flat kind.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate carries 5 visible tones per tile. That is above the grass reference (3) and below the paving reference (7). Near-flat coverage is 1%, so there are no large flat fills, and the speckle on both the dirt and the asphalt breaks up the surfaces. Only 3% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so the edges are a darker version of the neighbouring material (a darker brown or grey ledge), not a black sticker line. Each material has about 3-4 steps, a bit shallower than Beodeul's 5-6, and the asphalt is somewhat plain. Against the grass reference, which is similarly sparse in visible tones, it holds up as ground and would not look thinner next to it.

The road is a flat plane with speckled texture and has no front-edge line, eave shadow or ellipse. styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has only 9 distinct colours in total. The dirt carries about 3 browns plus speckle flecks. The asphalt carries about 3 greys with sparse dither dots. That is roughly 4 steps per material against about 6 on the Beodeul paving, and the asphalt reads as a mottled mid-grey mass. The measured facts are acceptable: 5 visible tones per tile (grass reference 3, paving reference 7), 1% near-flat coverage, and only 3% neutral dark edge pixels, so the edges are tinted rather than a near-black sticker line. The weaknesses are structural. The asphalt edge has no distinct broken lighter lip or per-chunk highlights, and no dark ledge is visible. The inner corner of the L reads as a sharp, hard-edged step rather than a soft chipped, rounded bite. Compared with the reference paving, which shades each stone with light and dark edges, the asphalt looks thinner and flatter. With the shading depth slightly short of the references and the edge detail missing, I fail it on a close call.
